title: Practice, and Erroll Garner's advice to play what you feel
summary: Wilson offers the Carnegie Hall joke, then contrasts Erroll Garner's individuality with Bud Powell copying Parker.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Well, I suppose I could borrow some remarks that have impressed me over the years, like the one about the guy who asks which is the quickest way to Carnegie Hall? Practice! That one is solid, that's a good thing to know.

And then the other thing that always impressed me, the pianist Erroll Garner used to say -- Garner came up in the bebop movement with Charlie Parker and Dizzy and all those guys dominated, on 52nd Street, and the piano players of that period like Bud Powell, Al Haig -- and Dorothy Donzgan was around there, a young kid from Chicago, and George Shearing came from England, and Erroll Garner came from Pittsburgh, and Erroll didn't get swallowed up in that movement like a lot of them did. It was confused. Erroll just plays what he feels. And that's it -- play by ear what you feel, stay true to your feelings and you can't miss.
Before he died, he was the highest priced jazz piano player there was.

And, creative and inventive on his own; I think that was one thing that might have stood in Bud Powell's way, to slavishly translate Charlie Parker to the keyboard, for the approval of his peers. He got tremendous
approval of his peers to do it, but what happened to Bud Powell?

Like when I feel like Billie Holiday translating Armstrong to a girl's voice, that feeling -- maybe before she died, she might have found herself, she wasn't a carbon copy of Charlie Parker, but when you hear Bud, he was the leading exponent of the Charlie Parker type piano playing, playing Charlie Parker's ideas on the piano, and he should have been playing Bud Powell's ideas on the piano.

But Garner, you don't hear any carbon copies of Garner, now. You hear some old time funky blues piano playing that those guys were playing in the South years ago, some of them guitar players -- but he used to do what he feels, and just play what you feel. Play it by ear is what he always used to say.

And another thing I noticed that Garner would do, when he was really starting to develop that skill, he wouldn't shy away from any idea, whether he made it clean or not -- you could tell what he intended. He didn't shy away to play it safe.
